blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. Choose **one** day to buy a share and a **later** day to sell it. Return the largest profit you can make — or `0` if no trade makes money.

blocks.alt: A line chart of prices [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] over days 0 to 5. Buying at price 1 on day 1 and selling at price 6 on day 4 gives the largest profit, 5.

elements.text: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
elements.originalText: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

blocks.code:
Input:  prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
Output: 5     buy on day 1 (price 1), sell on day 4 (price 6)

Input:  prices = [7, 6, 4, 3, 1]
Output: 0     the price only falls, so don't trade

blocks.text: Order matters: in the first example the highest price is 7, but it comes **before** the lowest price, so you can't buy at 1 and sell at 7. And if every trade loses money, you simply don't trade — the answer is never negative.
1. Brute force: try every pair of days
For every buy day, try every later sell day and keep the biggest difference.

**Time O(n²), space O(1).** About 5 billion comparisons for 100,000 days. For each buy day, the inner loop is really just looking for the **highest price after it** — and it recomputes that from scratch every time.
2. Optimal: precompute the best selling price
Compute that "highest price from day i to the end" for every day **once**, walking backwards. Then each buy day needs a single subtraction.

blocks.alt: Prices [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]. Highest price from each day to the end: [7, 6, 6, 6, 6, 4], filled from right to left. Profit if bought that day: [0, 5, 1, 3, 0, 0]. The best is 5, buying on day 1.
blocks.caption: maxAfter[i] = max(prices[i], maxAfter[i + 1]), and buying on day i earns maxAfter[i] − prices[i].

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** Two passes instead of n² pairs. The only cost left is the extra array.
3. Best solution: remember the cheapest day so far

Flip the question around. Instead of asking "when should I buy?", pretend **today** is the day you sell. Then the best day to have bought is simply the **cheapest day before today** — one number, not an array.
So walk forward once, carrying `minPrice` (the cheapest price so far) and `maxProfit` (the best sale so far). Selling today earns `price - minPrice`; if that beats `maxProfit`, keep it.

blocks.alt: A table over days 0 to 5. Prices: 7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4. Cheapest so far: 7, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Profit if sold today: 0, 0, 4, 2, 5, 3. Best profit so far: 0, 0, 4, 4, 5, 5.
blocks.caption: Each column only needs the column before it — that's why two variables are enough.
The bars show the price on each day. Watch min move to every new low, and maxProfit grow only when selling today beats the best so far.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** One pass, two variables.

rows.approach: Brute force: try every pair of days
rows.timeWhy: Every buy day is paired with every later sell day: about **n²/2** pairs.
rows.spaceWhy: Just the best profit and two indexes.

rows.approach: Optimal: precompute the best selling price
rows.timeWhy: **Two passes**: one builds the max-to-the-right array, one reads it.
rows.spaceWhy: An **extra array** with one entry per day.

rows.approach: Best: remember the cheapest day so far
rows.timeWhy: One pass, and each day does **O(1)** work.
rows.spaceWhy: Only **two variables**: the cheapest price and the best profit.

items: **One day** — `[5]` returns 0; you can't buy and sell on the same day.
**The best buy comes late** — `[3, 8, 2, 9]`: buying at 2 and selling at 9 beats buying at 3.

blocks.text: This is Kadane's algorithm in disguise: a trade's profit is the sum of the day-to-day price changes between buying and selling, so the best trade is the maximum subarray of those changes.
